{{Short description|Matrix with symbols that each occur once per row and column}}
In [[combinatorics|combinatorial mathematics]], a '''Latin rectangle''' is an {{math|''r''&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;''n''}} [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] (where {{math|''r''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n''}}), using {{mvar|n}} symbols, usually the numbers {{math|1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;3,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''n''}} or {{math|0, 1, ..., ''n'' − 1}} as its entries, with no number occurring more than once in any row or column.{{sfn|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=p. 141}}

An {{math|''n''&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;''n''}} Latin rectangle is called a [[Latin square]]. Latin rectangles and Latin squares may also be described as the optimal [[graph coloring|colorings]] of [[rook's graph]]s, or as optimal [[edge coloring]]s of [[complete bipartite graph]]s.{{sfn|Stones|2010}}

An example of a 3 × 5 Latin rectangle is:<ref>{{harvnb|Brualdi|2010|loc=p. 385}}</ref>

:{| class="wikitable"
|-
|0|| 1|| 2|| 3|| 4
|-
|3|| 4 ||0 ||1|| 2
|-
|4|| 0|| 3|| 2|| 1
|}

==Normalization==
A Latin rectangle is called ''normalized'' (or ''reduced'') if its first row is in natural order and so is its first column.<ref name=DK150>{{harvnb|Dénes|Keedwell|1974|loc=p. 150}}</ref><ref>Some authors, notably J. Riordan, do not require the first column to be in order and this will effect the validity of some formulas mentioned below.</ref>

The example above is not normalized.

==Enumeration==

Let {{mvar|L}}({{mvar|k, n}}) denote the number of normalized {{mvar|k}} × {{mvar|n}} Latin rectangles. Then the total number of {{mvar|k}} × {{mvar|n}} Latin rectangles is<ref name=CD142>{{harvnb|Colbourn|Dinitz|2007|loc=p. 142}}</ref>
:<math>\frac{n! (n-1)! L(k,n)}{(n-k)!}.</math>

A 2 × {{mvar|n}} Latin rectangle corresponds to a [[permutation]] with no [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed points]]. Such permutations have been called ''discordant permutations''.<ref name=DK150 /> An enumeration of permutations discordant with a given permutation is the famous [[problème des rencontres]]. The enumeration of permutations discordant with two permutations, one of which is a simple cyclic shift of the other, is known as the reduced [[problème des ménages]].<ref name=DK150 />

The number of normalized Latin rectangles, {{math|''L''(''k'', ''n'')}}, of small sizes is given by<ref name=CD142 />
:{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;"
|-
! k\n !!1!!2!!3!!4!!5!!6!!7!!8
|-
! 1 
|1||1||1||1||1||1||1||1
|- 
! 2 
| ||1||1||3||11||53||309||2119
|-
! 3 
| || ||1||4||46||1064||35792||1673792
|-
! 4 
| || || ||4||56||6552||1293216||420909504
|-
! 5 
| || || || ||56||9408||11270400||27206658048
|-
! 6 
| || || || || ||9408||16942080||335390189568
|-
! 7 
| || || || || || ||16942080||535281401856
|-
! 8
| || || || || || || ||535281401856
|}

When {{mvar|k}} = 1, that is, there is only one row, since the Latin rectangles are normalized there is no choice for what this row can be. The table also shows that {{math|1=''L''(''n'' &minus; 1, ''n'') = ''L''(''n'', ''n'')}}, which follows since if only one row is missing, the missing entry in each column can be determined from the [[Latin square property]] and the rectangle can be uniquely extended to a Latin square.

==Extendability==
The property of being able to extend a Latin rectangle missing one row to a Latin square mentioned above, can be significantly strengthened. Namely, if {{math|''r''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''n''}}, then it is possible to append {{math|''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''r''}} rows to an {{math|''r''&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;''n''}} Latin rectangle to form a Latin square, using [[Hall's marriage theorem]].<ref>{{harvnb|Brualdi|2010|loc=p. 386}}</ref>

==Semi-Latin squares==
A semi-Latin square is another type of incomplete Latin square. A '''semi-Latin square''' is an {{mvar|n}} × {{mvar|n}} array, {{mvar|L}}, in which some positions are unoccupied and other positions are occupied by one of the integers {{math|{0, 1, ..., ''n'' − 1}}}, such that, if an integer {{mvar|k}} occurs in {{mvar|L}}, then it occurs {{mvar|n}} times and no two {{mvar|k}}'s belong to the same row or column. If {{mvar|m}} different integers occur in {{mvar|L}}, then {{mvar|L}} has ''index'' {{mvar|m}}.<ref name=Bru387>{{harvnb|Brualdi|2010|loc=p. 387}}</ref>

For example, a semi-Latin square of order 5 and index 3 is:<ref name=Bru387 />
:{| class="wikitable"
|-
| 1 ||   || 0 ||   || 2
|-
|   || 2 || 1 ||   || 0
|-
| 0 || 1 ||   || 2 ||  
|-
| 2 || 0 ||   || 1 ||  
|-
|   ||   || 2 || 0 || 1
|}

A semi-Latin square of order {{mvar|n}} and index {{mvar|m}} will have {{mvar|nm}} filled positions. The question arises, can a semi-Latin square be completed to a Latin square? Somewhat surprisingly, the answer is always.

Let {{mvar|L}} be a semi-Latin square of order {{mvar|n}} and index {{mvar|m}}, where {{mvar|m < n}}. Then {{mvar|L}} can be completed to a Latin square.<ref name=Bru387 />

One way to prove this is to observe that a semi-Latin square of order {{mvar|n}} and index {{mvar|m}} is equivalent to an {{mvar|m}} × {{mvar|n}} Latin rectangle. Let {{math|1=''L'' = {{!}}{{!}}''a''<sub>''ij''</sub>{{!}}{{!}}}} be a Latin rectangle and {{math|1=''S'' = {{!}}{{!}}''b''<sub>''ij''</sub>{{!}}{{!}}}} be a semi-Latin square, then the equivalence is given by<ref name=Bru388>{{harvnb|Brualdi|2010|loc=p. 388}}</ref>
:<math>b_{ij} = k \text{  if and only if  } a_{kj} = i.</math>
For instance, the 3×5 Latin rectangle
:{| class="wikitable"
|-
| 0 || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4
|-
| 3 || 4 || 1 || 0 || 2
|-
| 1 || 0 || 4 || 2 || 3
|}
is equivalent to this semi-Latin square of order 5 and index 3:<ref name=Bru388 />
:{| class="wikitable"
|-
| 0 || 2 ||  || 1 ||  
|-
| 2 || 0 || 1 ||   ||  
|-
|   ||   || 0 || 2 || 1
|-
| 1 ||   ||   || 0 || 2
|-
|   || 1 || 2 ||   || 0
|}
since, for example, {{mvar|a}}<sub>10</sub> = 3 in the Latin rectangle so {{mvar|b}}<sub>30</sub> = 1 in the semi-Latin square.

==Applications==
In [[statistics]], Latin rectangles have applications in the [[design of experiments]].{{how?|date=July 2024}}
